text:
Andy Burnham has launched a Hillsborough-style investigation to examine a programme of blood tests on service personnel during nuclear weapons trials, which he said had been the subject of a “criminal cover-up on an industrial scale”.
The Ministry of Defence admitted conducting biological examinations on troops exposed to nuclear testing, having denied it to parliament and the courts for decades. In September, the former defence minister Tobias Ellwood admitted to unwittingly misleading parliament in 2018 over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans.
James Jones, the former bishop of Liverpool, who chaired the Hillsborough panel, will chair the independent panel into nuclear test veterans. The panel will follow the same model and will aim to produce an interim report in time for the 75th anniversary of the first UK nuclear weapons test.
Between 1952 and 1967, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific. Some pilots flew through mushroom clouds, some troops crawled through fallout, and many witnesses of the first bomb test were wearing short-sleeved shirts and shorts.
Large numbers later suffered blood disorders and cancers, which they believed were caused by exposure to radioactive fallout. Most were denied pensions because of their ill health.
Burnham, who as mayor of Greater Manchester in June 2024 said the MoD was “bang to rights”, said Jones would be “relentless” in his pursuit of the facts.
“I pay tribute to the courage and dedication of the community and campaigners. This announcement is the result of their tireless work,” he said. “Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish.”
The move was cheered by veterans, who have been fighting for decades to see the records as many look to prove that their serious illnesses were linked to their experiences testing nuclear weapons.
Alan Owen, the founder of Labrats International, one of the leading organisations representing nuclear bomb test veterans, said it recognised the efforts of the prime minister and his team to listen to the community and take its concerns seriously.
“This progress has not happened overnight. It is the result of years of determined campaigning and constructive engagement between Labrats and the Office for Veterans’ Affairs,” he said.
“Today, we also want to pay tribute to the many campaigners who came before us, who fought tirelessly for recognition and justice but sadly did not live to see the progress announced today. We stand on their shoulders. Their courage, determination and unwavering commitment laid the foundations for what we have achieved, and we owe it to them to finish what they started.”
The Hillsborough law, officially called the public office (accountability) bill, is in the report stage in parliament, and when it becomes law in early 2027 it will impose a duty of candour on public officials and bodies and create a new criminal offence of misleading the public.
Government sources said Burnham had been clear that “he expects the government to act in the spirit of that duty straight away”, adding that he would work with the Cabinet Office to work with the veteran community on education, research and memorialisation.

ראש ממשלת בריטניה, אנדי ברנהם, הכריז על הקמת ועדת חקירה עצמאית בראשות ג'יימס ג'ונס שתבחן את תוכנית בדיקות הדם שנערכו לאנשי צבא במהלך ניסויי נשק גרעיני. הממשלה הודתה כי בוצעו בדיקות ביולוגיות על חיילים שנחשפו לנשורת רדיואקטיבית, זאת לאחר שדבריו של שר ההגנה לשעבר חשפו כי הפרלמנט הוטעה בנושא במשך עשורים.

בין השנים 1952 ל-1967 השתתפו כ-22,000 אנשי צבא בריטיים בעשרות ניסויים גרעיניים באוסטרליה ובדרום האוקיינוס השקט, ורבים מהם חלו במחלות קשות בהמשך חייהם. ועדת החקירה החדשה תפעל במתכונת דומה לוועדת הילזבורו, במטרה לחשוף את האמת ולהגיש דו
